content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work studies the loss landscape of a deep nonlinear model with generic activations

The paper shows that bad minima can exist under quite general conditions (if my understanding is correct)
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. the results feel novel, and the proposed technique of local minimum embedding seems to have great promise
2. one interesting insight that the main results offer is that the existence of local minimum can crucially depend on the dataset size N, even when N is very small, which I find interesting

The following are the weaknesses that the authors should address:

1. Clarifying questions: 
- according to def 1, is every nonattracting local minimum a global minimum?
- what is the difference between a local minimum and a local valley?

2. There seems to be a lot of missing conditions/definition for the problem setup. For example, all the results are proved without any assumption/specification of the loss function $\ell$, and I do not think the results can be proved without assuming some well-behaving condition for $\ell$.
- for example, to prove proposition 1, the authors at least need to assume in the proposition statement that a "linear minimizer" exists
- more on prop 1, the result is actually about a two-layer model, but this is not clearly stated in the proposition
- prop 2: one needs to assume that the loss function in $\hat{Y}$ is strongly convex (or some similar condition)
- prop 4: "strict local minimum" not defined
- assumption 1: the colloquial word "actually" is very confusing -- is the statement regarding eq 6 an assumption or a consequence of the assumption?

3. Missing references and discussion
- an old work that studies one-layer models should be discussed: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/epl/i1998-00466-6
- a recent work that studies bad minima in deep linear nets with regularization is also relevant and should be discussed: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04777
- How do the results in this paper change if an L2 regularization is added?


4. There seem to be too many typos and grammatical errors
- I actually suggest that the authors seriously check the English of the present paper and resubmit to another conference

5. the authors should present at least some minimal numerical examples to illustrate the results

Minor:
1. typo on page 3: "if a property... if it holds..."
2. page 4: "does a bad local minimum is discovered?"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity is hugely hindered by the poor English of the paper. For a theory paper like this, clarity is of utmost importance.

The novelty is good, in my opinion. One interesting implication of the paper is that the existence of bad minima can depend on the dataset size, which is an interesting discovery

The proposed technique of local minimum embedding also seems very promising. But def 2 is virtually unreadable. I suggest that the authors break it down into a few pieces to improve readability and comprehensibility.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This work studies the loss landscape of a deep nonlinear model with generic activations and shows great theoretical promise. The results are also novel.

However, I cannot recommend acceptance at this stage because the writing and the presentation is poor: 
1. the statements of the theorems and definitions are ambiguous and unclear, often with missing conditions and undefined terms
2. the English also needs improvement
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provided a constructive proof showing the existence of bad local minima of 2-layer and 3-layer neural networks with general smooth activations and square loss. The assumptions include the input and output being scalars, the number of samples being at least some constant, and some non-degeneracy assumptions on the activation function. The construction of bad local minima works for a positive-measure set of (input, label) pairs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
-Strengths:

1. This paper introduces new techniques from differential Galois theory to extend previous results to general smooth activation functions, including most commonly-used activations.

2. The notations and settings are formally defined in this paper, and the related works are mostly properly cited. The theoretical results in this paper appear to be correct.

-Weaknesses:

1. The theoretical results in this paper might be somewhat restricted, and I will provide the details below:

1.1 The construction of the bad local minima in this paper requires selecting the labels for the input data, i.e., it does not work for general labels. Although the authors further showed that the selection of the labels has a positive measure, they did not provide a lower bound on the measure and this measure seems very small. Therefore, this construction may not work for most (input, label) pairs.

1.2 It might be very difficult to extend the result to deeper neural networks. The requirement on sample size, i.e., the size of the set $B$, grows fast as the number of layers increases. Therefore, the sample size requirement may quickly become unrealistic when the network gets deeper. Furthermore, the difficulty of verifying the linear independence in set $B$ grows with the size of $B$.

1.3 The results in this paper only hold for scalar inputs, which is restrictive if it cannot be easily extended to multi-dimensional inputs.

2. The organization of the sections and proofs seems somewhat confusing, and this paper might need a major revision to improve its clarity. The proof of all lemmas and propositions are in the appendix without providing a proof sketch in the main text, making it hard to understand the ideas and insights behind these results. Besides, some sentences and equations can be simplified. There are also some typos in the formulas and texts. The details will be provided in the "Clarity" part in the next section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
-Quality and Reproducibility: The notations and settings in this paper are formally and clearly defined, and the theoretical results appear to be correct. The theoretical proofs are given in the appendix in detail, making it easy to verify.

-Novelty: To the best of my knowledge, the application of differential Galois theory to the construction of bad local minima in neural network landscape is novel. The related works are adequately cited, with the most related ones listed in Table 1 and clearly compared.

-Clarity: This paper does not seem to be very well-written and might need a major revision. As mentioned in the "Weakness" section, the authors did not provide proof or proof sketch in the main text, some expressions could be simplified, and there are some typos. I will discuss these three parts separately below:

(1) Proof/Proof sketch:

It could be hard to fully understand the implications and insights of a conclusion without knowing the proof idea. Therefore, it would be better to provide at least a proof sketch for the important conclusion in this paper so that the readers can have a better understanding. The current version of this paper uses a proof environment that occupies much space and provides only a pointer to the appendix. I would recommend the authors use the space to provide some proof ideas and put the pointer into plain text to save space.

(2) Simplifying things:

Some formulas or expressions may not be completely necessary for the understanding of the main idea of this paper, so some details about them can be moved into the appendix. For example, the detailed expressions for the seven activation functions may not be that important, and Definition 1 can be merged into one sentence.

(3) Typos/Minors:

-Section 3, paragraph 2, "$N$-layer" -> "$L$-layer", "$W_N, b_N$" -> "$W_L, b_L$", "$d_Y\times d_N$" -> "d_Y\times d_L"

-Section 3, paragraph 6, "If a property $P$" -> "A property $P$"

-Theorem 1, "$(t_0,y_0)\in D$ $(t_0,y_0)\in D$" -> "$(t_0,y_0)\in D$"

-paragraph after Theorem 1, "freedom, Hence the solution set of 6" -> "freedom, the solution set of (6)"

-Definition 2, "the weights of the smaller network $W^{large}$" -> "the weights of the smaller network $W^{small}$", "where $\bar{W}^{small}$ denote the collection of all remaining weights of the smaller network" is duplicated twice.

-Remark 2, "independent the embedding" -> "independent of the embedding"
content.summary_of_the_review: I tend to vote for rejecting this paper. Despite introducing differential Galois theory to extend previous construction of spurious local minima to general smooth activation functions, the results in this paper are somewhat restricted because of the requirements for the labels, network depth, input dimension, and potentially sample size. The clarity of this paper could also need major improvements.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer rCRJ
content.comment:
We appreciate your insightful and constructive comments. 

First of all, we would like to apologize for several typos in the paper. We corrected these typos in the revised version. 

We understand the concerns of the reviewer. 
We agree that it is important to provide a lower bound of a positive measure. However, even if a positive measure is small, we think that it is a meaningful result because a positive measure implies a scenario is likely to happen. 

We also agree that the size of B increases as the number of layers increases. This indicates that the required sample sizes can be very large for a very deep network. We believe that it could be an implication of the absence of a bad local minimum for the very deep network. 

Additionally, we are very grateful for the advice on the structure of the paper. We plan to revise the paper in a future version based on the reviewer's comments.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the existence of bad local minima (i.e., local minima that are not globally optimal) for neural networks equipped with general smooth activation functions. The paper proves several non-existence and existence theorems for bad local minima. Using $N$ to denote the number of data points, the key contributions of the paper are:

- For $N=1, 2$ and 2-layer network of width 1, there is no bad local minimum (Propositions 2 and 3)
- For $N \geq 7$, squared error loss, and a 2-layer network of width $\geq 2$ there is a bad local minimum (Theorem 3). The class of datasets $(X,Y)$ for which the theorem holds has a positive measure. 
- For $N \geq 34$, squared error loss, and a 3-layer network of width $\geq 2$ there is a bad local minimum (Theorem 4). The class of datasets $(X,Y)$ for which the theorem holds has a positive measure.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Understanding the existence of bad local minima is an important topic. Some existing results are indeed limited to sigmoidal activations, hence an attempt to expand our understanding on this topic to general smooth activation functions is valuable.

- However, in my opinion, many of the results presented in this paper lack novelty and the quality of writing has a lot to be desired. I also believe that in some parts of the paper, comparisons to existing results are not done properly. Allow me to elaborate in the comments below.

- Many of the proposition/theorem statements are not stated fully completely. For example, in Propositions 2 and 3, it seems from the proof that $d_X = d_1 = d_Y = 1$ but the statement only says $d_X = d_1 = d_Y$. Also, the proofs of the propositions also use some properties of the activation function e.g., existence of $\sigma^{-1}(y_1)$ and $\sigma'(x) > 0$. So naturally there must have been at least some assumptions on the activation $\sigma$, which are absent in the statements. Also in Proposition 3, why is the loss $\ell$ a function of only $x$ and what is $x$? In Eq (4) $\ell$ has two arguments. The proof also seems to leverage the fact that $\ell$ is a function of $y - f(x)$ (the equation right above Eq (33)), but why do we *not* have any of these assumptions? In Proposition 4, why doesn't the statement say anything about $Y$?

- For Propositions 2 and 3, the arXiv version (I don't have access to their final version at Mathematics of OR) of Ding et al (2022) has Theorems 4 and 5 which also show nonexistence of bad local minima for $N = 1,2$. The paper does not mention this nor compare against these existing results. I consider it a bad omission.

- Propositions 4 and 5 establish the existence of a strict local minimum, and by adding additional neurons to the hidden layer, the paper establishes in Theorem 3 that these local minima (extended to the larger network) are not globally optimal. Here, the technique used to jump from Propositions 4 & 5 to Theorem 3 relies heavily on the tools developed in Petzka & Sminchisescu (2021). Specifically, the important part that proves that the local minimum is actually *nonoptimal/bad* is the same as the existing paper. Same goes for the step from Proposition 6 to Theorem 4.

- Hence, to me, it looks like the main technical contributions of this paper are defining Assumptions 1 and 2 for the activation functions, and for those activations, constructing output values $Y$ (for a given $X$) that induce strict local minima (Propositions 4–6). Although I value the technicalities involved in proving e.g., Lemma 1, I am not fully convinced if these alone can merit acceptance.

- As a side question, the authors claim that the existing paper Ding et al (2022) and Petzka & Sminchisescu (2021) rely on the properties of sigmoid activation function that must be verified experimentally. As a person who had carefully read both papers a while ago, I couldn't see exactly which part of these papers required experimental verifications. Could you elaborate?

Minor points:
- In Eq (1), $X$ -> $X_i$. By the way $F_L$ is a bad choice of notation because it does not show any dependence on the index $i$.
- In Eq (2), is there any reason why the bias vector is applied *after* $\sigma$?
- What is the purpose of Proposition 1 by the way? It seems that it's not used anywhere else in the paper, and it doesn't show any existence of bad local minima. Am I mistaken?
- In Assumption 1, the set $B$ and the coefficient $B$ have overloading notation.
- By the way, Definition 2 looks just overwhelming/unreadable and I think this complexity is unnecessary. It is nothing but "splitting" a neuron in the $l$-th layer; one can find a better way to define the term "local minimum embedding." Indeed, there are many typos in the definition, e.g., "smaller network $W^{large}$".
- Theorem 4 requires $N \geq 34$ while Section 1 says it's $N \geq 29$.
- In Sec A.1.3, after "For the training samples $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)$", $F_1(W,x_1)$ in the matrix should be $\sigma(F_1(W,x_1))$. Also, starting from "Suppose $F_1(W,x_1) < y_1$", $F_1$'s should be corrected to $F_2$'s.
- In Sec A.2.2, there are places where $x$ must be corrected to $x_i$, see e.g., Eq (69) or the line after Eq (57).
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem that the paper tries to solve is valuable, but to me the key contributions of the paper look rather incremental. Due to the criticisms listed above, I recommend rejection.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to  Reviewer SbAd
content.comment:
We appreciate your thorough review and constructive comments. 

First of all, we would like to apologize for several typos in the paper. We corrected these typos in the revised version. 

We decided to delete the section dealing with small sample sizes (N=1,2). Initially, we include them for a story of local minimum, but because they are not our main contribution, we thought this might make confusion about contributions (we referred to the journal version of Ding et al (2022)).

For the side question, we think that there are numerical verification parts in the proofs [A] Ding et al., 2022 and [B] Petzka & Sminchisescu, 2021. In [A], the authors of [A] show that the sigmoid function satisfies Assumption 1 by showing that 7x7 the matrix [B(1),B(2), ... B(7)] is not singular by numerical calculation. In [B], the authors in [B] find a critical point of the specific narrow network for synthesized data via gradient descent. After calculating the eigenvalues of the Hessian, they verify that the found critical point is a local minimum. For this reason, we thought that the proofs in both papers require numerical verifications. However, if a proof requires numerical verifications, it cannot work for general activations, since the experiments cannot be conducted infinitely. So we think that a purely mathematical proof is needed.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the loss landscape of fully-connected neural networks. The main contribution is to construct bad local minima for 2-layer and 3-layer networks for positive-measure training data. The main idea consists of two steps:
1) Construct strict local minima for narrow networks with only one neuron in each hidden layer
2) By local minimum embedding, show that arbitrarily wide networks have bad local minima.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

This paper shows that neural networks with non-linear smooth activations have local minima for positive-measure data (for both input X and output Y).  The best result for positive-measure data in the prior work only holds for 2-layer networks with sigmoid activation. In that sense, this paper goes one step forward by extending the result to 3-layer networks and general smooth activations. 

This result implies that bad local minima may exist for non-negligible training data, leading to potential training difficulties.

 
### Weakness

The proof combines and extends the techniques used in [A] Ding et al., 2022 and [B] Petzka & Sminchisescu, 2021. However, 

**1. The prior work [A] is not properly cited.**

First, [A] has two main results. It constructed bad local minima for 
- general nonlinear smooth activations for networks with almost arbitrary depth and width (for generic X and constructed Y);
- sigmoid activation for 2-layer networks (for positive-measure X and Y).

Only the second result is mentioned in the introduction and Table 1, which severely undervalues the contribution of [A].

Second, many proof ideas are borrowed from [A] without proper acknowledgment. For example, 
- the linear independence assumption (Assumption 1) is the same with [A] (Assumption 1, for d_x = 1)
- the construction of strict local minima for 2-layer networks (Proposition 4) is the same as [A] (Theorem 2)


**2. The proof has a cavity.**

Note that a strict local minimum not necessarily implies a positive-definite (PD) Hessian matrix, but only implies a positive semidefinite (PSD) Hessian. For example, x=0 is a strict local minimum of f(x)=x^4, but the Hessian is 0. Thus, several proofs are problematic in this paper:

- The second part of Lemma 2 where the authors claim that the local minimum after perturbation is strict.
- The proof of Theorem 3 and 4 is not rigorous, since the local minimum embedding technique in Petzka & Sminchisescu, 2021 requires PD Hessian.

To fix this, the authors need to show that the local minima constructed for narrow networks (both 2-layer and 3-layer) have PD Hessian, which is not straightforward to me.

**3. The proof techniques do not provide much new insight given [A] and [B].**

First, the 2-layer case seems a direct extension of [A, Theorem 2]. Although [A, Theorem 2] only holds for sigmoid activation, the only property of sigmoid used in the proof is Assumption 1. This paper shows that most smooth activations satisfy Assumption 1 (which is a contribution), and hence [A, Theorem 2] can be directly extended to most smooth activations. 

Second, the idea of finding a local minimum for a narrow network and then generalizing it to wide networks has already been presented in [B]. The embedding techniques are completely the same as [B].

Given the prior works, the major technical contributions of this paper are:
- show that most smooth activations satisfy Assumption 1;
- construct a strict local minimum for the 3-layer network with width 1.
From my point of view, this is not sufficient to support an ICLR publication.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The idea is clearly presented, but the proof has a cavity. 

This paper combines and extends several techniques in prior works. The construction of strict local-min for narrow 3-layer networks is of certain novelty, but the 2-layer case is a direct extension of existing results.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Main contribution: 
First work to construct bad local-min for 2-layer and 3-layer networks with positive-measure data and general smooth activations.

Major Weakness: 
1) Not properly citing an existing work; 
2) A Cavity is found in the proof; 
3) Marginal novelty in the proof techniques.

Suggestion: Reject
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2585 by Reviewer Nn41

content.title: Response to Reviewer Nn41
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback. Your review is very helpful in improving the paper. 

Comment 1:  The prior work [A] is not properly cited.

Answer: We will properly cite the works the reviewer mentioned in the main text and tables. In the proof, we will appropriately mention the ideas borrowed from the other works. 

Comment 2: The proof has a cavity.

Answer: We really appreciate the reviewer pointing out the crucial cavity in the proof. As the reviewer pointed out, the statement of Lemma 4 was not accurate. So we corrected the condition of the lemma from strict local minimum to strict local minimum "with strictly positive definite Hessian". Then, we complete the proof by showing the Hessian of the constructed local minimum is strictly positive definite. Since we found some gaps in other proofs, we complete the proof by complementing the gaps in the revised version.

Comment 3: The proof techniques do not provide much new insight given [A] Ding et al., 2022 and [B] Petzka & Sminchisescu, 2021. 

Answer: We agree that we used several techniques presented in [A] and [B] in the r proof. However, we claim that our work has the following contributions. 
 - We extend the result of [A] from a single function to a general analytic function.  

This might be considered a simple extension, but since even very elementary functions such as e^x and sin(x) do not satisfy the assumption, it is important to find a general criterion about the activations in order to analyze complicated activation functions such as GELU or Mish. Moreover, with the criterion, we think we found a way to extend from 2-layer to the deeper networks.
